source.title: Confidence Adaptive Regularization for Deep Learning with Noisy Labels
source.authors: Yangdi Lu; Yang Bo; Wen-Bo He

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures learning over training for clean and corrupted labels, using ResNet34 and a different loss or learning-rate schedule than the original sources.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports the fraction of clean-label samples predicted correctly and false-label samples predicted correctly, memorized, or predicted as neither, across training epochs. Table 1 and other comparison tables report results from prior papers for the other methods; those cited results are excluded.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 directly measures V6 using training trajectories for clean and mislabeled examples. Cross-entropy baselines learn true labels before memorizing false labels; CAR measures whether this behavior persists under a targeted intervention.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete: the authors exploit early learning through confidence-dependent loss and target correction to prevent noisy-label memorization, and report competitive classification performance across synthetic and real-world noisy datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tracks clean and noisy-label predictions over training, but uses 40% symmetric noise and also evaluates CAR and multiple learning-rate schedules rather than testing completely random labels under unchanged settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The false-label memorization rate depends on the learning-rate schedule: Cosine Annealing slows it relative to MultiStep. CAR with Cosine Annealing is described as preventing it.

fits_no_version.finding: Confidence distributions, label-correction accuracy, and robust-method test accuracy measure confidence separation or mitigation performance rather than the claimed learning sequence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CAR can distinguish and correct mislabeled samples and improve classification under label noise.

record.problems: Figure 1 results are presented graphically, with no numerical values or uncertainty reported in the text. The temporal comparison is for one architecture, one dataset, and one 40% symmetric noise setting.
record.rows_left_out: No other eligible results were left out. Comparison-table results for other methods are explicitly taken from their original papers and are not this study's own results.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time ratio for random versus true labels and convergence time across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit together with test-error progression across a corruption sweep from none to all. Test-accuracy tables alone do not establish this joint claim.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent fitting completely random labels, and generalization after removing these regularizers.

Completely random labels and direct temporal comparisons beyond ResNet34 on CIFAR-10 with 40% symmetric noise. The CIFAR-100 qualification is qualitative and supported by confidence distributions rather than comparable learning trajectories.

missing.what: The authors' qualitative observation that early learning is less evident on datasets with many classes, illustrated by nearby clean/noisy confidence distributions on CIFAR-100. Record the proxy-measure limitation explicitly.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text supports qualitative trajectory states but does not provide readable Figure 1 values. Training lasts 500 epochs to check for delayed memorization. Figure 3 supplies gradient evidence consistent with Figure 1, but gradients alone do not measure the claimed behavior. Other methods' cited comparison-table results are excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, and comparison without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training-time cost relative to true labels and convergence time as corruption fraction changes.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The study uses 40% symmetric label noise in Figure 1, but does not report perfect training fit and test-error progression across a sweep from no noise to all labels corrupted.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation fail to prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them worsens true-label generalization.
The study examines 40% symmetric noisy labels, not completely random labels, and does not test whether this ordering holds across other models or settings.

rows.note: The text says Cosine Annealing only slows the speed of memorizing false labels; precise values are shown only in the figure.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Confidence Adaptive Regularization and a Cosine Annealing learning-rate scheduler; tracked predictions over epochs.
rows.measure: Fraction of clean-label samples predicted correctly over epochs
rows.note: The text says all three models predict clean-label samples correctly as epochs increase; precise values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: Observed applies to clean-label learning, not the complete early-learning/later-memorization sequence. The subject includes an added indicator branch and target correction; CIFAR-10 uses beta=0, so the auxiliary regularizer is inactive.

source_check.correct: state: cannot_determine for V6 from clean-label accuracy alone; clean-label learning continues, while R6 reports prevention of false-label memorization.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Confidence Adaptive Regularization and a Cosine Annealing learning-rate scheduler; tracked predictions over epochs.
rows.measure: Fraction of false-label samples memorized over epochs
rows.note: The authors say their approach effectively prevents memorization of false labels; precise values are shown only in the figure.
